think.q: "A component re-renders only when its props change." True?
opts: No, by default it re-renders whenever its parent does
why: memo() is what adds the props check.

think.q: How do you see why something rendered?
opts: React DevTools Profiler with "Record why each component rendered" enabled
why: Measure before optimising.

try.task: Fix a slow page by moving state down. Page({ onRowRender }) renders a search <input> and a <BigList onRender={onRowRender} /> (50 rows that call onRender each time they render). Typing in the search must not re-render the list.
examples: type 3 letters → onRowRender not called again
the input still shows what you typed
try.hint: Move the input and its state into its own SearchBox component; Page itself keeps no state.

checks.t: typing does not re-render the list

takeaway.key: Components re-render on own state, parent render, or context change. Move state down or pass components as children before reaching for memo.
mistakes: Keeping fast-changing state high in the tree.

think.q: Is wrapping every component in memo() a good default?
opts: No: comparing props costs time too, and most renders are cheap
why: Use it where profiling shows an expensive subtree.

think.q: A memo() component reads a context that changes. Does memo stop the re-render?
opts: No, context changes always re-render consumers
why: memo only checks props.

try.task: Make a list cheap to update: TodoList({ todos, onToggle, onRowRender }) renders a memoized TodoRow per todo (a checkbox calling onToggle(id)). When one todo changes, only that row may re-render.
examples: toggle todo 2 of 3 → onRowRender called once more, for row 2
the parent passes a stable onToggle (useCallback)
try.hint: TodoRow = memo(...); rows get primitive props or the todo object itself (unchanged todos keep their reference); onToggle must be stable.

takeaway.key: memo() skips renders when all props are Object.is-equal. Keep props stable (primitives, unchanged objects, useCallback), and use it where it measurably helps.
mistakes: Custom compare functions that hide real changes.

think.q: With the React Compiler enabled, what happens to this triad?
opts: The compiler inserts the memoization automatically, so most manual memo/useMemo/useCallback can go
why: Understanding the triad still helps you read code and debug.

think.q: Which should you try first for a slow subtree?
opts: Restructure (move state down, pass children) before adding memoization
why: Structure fixes are free; memoization has costs.

try.task: Write Dashboard({ rows, onChartRender }): holds a theme toggle button and renders a memoized Chart with props points (rows mapped to r.value) and onPick. Toggling the theme must not re-render Chart; Chart calls onChartRender() each render and shows the point count.
examples: toggle theme 3 times → onChartRender called once
<output> inside Chart shows the number of points
try.hint: Chart = memo(...); points = useMemo(() => rows.map(...), [rows]); onPick = useCallback(...).

checks.t: toggling theme does not re-render the chart

takeaway.key: memo (child) + useMemo (object/array props) + useCallback (function props) only work together. Restructure first; the React Compiler can automate this.
mistakes: Adding useCallback without memo on the child.

think.q: Why does passing <Heavy /> as children avoid its re-render?
opts: The element object comes from the parent's render; if that render did not run, it is the same object and React skips it
why: Same element reference = nothing to do.

think.q: Before reaching for memo(), what should you try?
opts: Moving state down or lifting content up with children/slots
why: They are free and make the structure clearer.

try.task: Write ExpandablePanel({ title, children }): a header button (starts open) toggles open/closed (aria-expanded) and shows a click count; children stay mounted but are hidden with the hidden attribute when closed, and toggling must not re-render the children that were passed in.
examples: toggle twice → Heavy still rendered only once
try.hint: Keep the open state in the panel and render <div hidden={!open}>{children}</div>. Unmounting with {open && children} would remount them. Children created by the caller keep their identity, so the panel's own re-renders skip them.

checks.t: toggling does not re-render passed-in children

takeaway.key: Move state down and lift content up (children/slots). Elements created by an outer component are reused when an inner one re-renders.
mistakes: Creating expensive children inside a frequently updating component.

think.q: lazy(() => import("./Chart")) fails with "Element type is invalid". Likely cause?
opts: Chart.jsx has only a named export; lazy needs a module with a default export (or map it: .then(m => ({ default: m.Chart })))
why: lazy expects { default: Component }.

think.q: Best first place to code-split a typical app?
opts: Routes: each page becomes its own chunk
why: Route boundaries give the biggest win for the least complexity.

think.q: How can you hide the loading delay of a lazy route?
opts: Start the import early (on hover/intent) so the chunk is cached before the click
why: Calling the import function once warms the cache.

try.task: Write lazyWithPreload(factory): like lazy(factory) but the returned component also has a .preload() method that starts loading early; factory must run at most once.
try.hint: Cache the promise: let p; const load = () => (p ??= factory()); const C = lazy(load); C.preload = load.

takeaway.key: lazy() + import() + Suspense = load code on demand. Split routes first, preload on intent, and remember lazy needs a default export.
mistakes: Splitting tiny components (more requests, no gain).
No Suspense boundary above a lazy component.

dryRun.title: 10,000 rows, 40 px each, viewport 400 px, scrollTop 4000
dryRun.note: Virtualization (windowing) renders only the rows in view (plus a few extra) inside a tall spacer, positioning them with a transform or top offset. DOM size stays tiny no matter how long the list is. Libraries: TanStack Virtual, react-window.

think.q: What problem does virtualization solve?
opts: Thousands of DOM nodes make rendering, layout and memory slow; only visible rows are rendered
why: The DOM is the expensive part.

think.q: What breaks with naive virtualization?
opts: Ctrl+F browser search and anchor links to off-screen rows (they are not in the DOM)
why: Mention this trade-off in interviews.

think.q: Rows have different heights. What does a virtualizer need?
opts: Measured or estimated sizes, with a cache of real heights once rendered
why: TanStack Virtual measures elements as they render.

think.q: Why render a few extra rows above and below the viewport?
opts: So fast scrolling does not flash blank space before new rows render
why: A small overscan hides the render gap.

think.q: When is virtualization overkill?
opts: A chat with years of messages
why: Measure: a few hundred simple rows are usually fine.

try.task: Write the math of a virtual list: getVirtualRange({ count, itemHeight, viewportHeight, scrollTop, overscan = 3 }) returning { start, end, offsetTop, totalHeight } (end exclusive, clamped to 0…count).
try.hint: first = floor(scrollTop / h); visible = ceil(viewport / h); start = max(0, first - overscan); end = min(count, first + visible + overscan); offsetTop = start * h.

checks.t: clamped at the bottom and tiny lists

takeaway.key: Render only visible rows (plus overscan) inside a full-height spacer. Mind variable heights and the loss of in-page search.
mistakes: No overscan → blank flashes when scrolling.

dryRun.note: Measure before you optimise. The React DevTools Profiler records commits and shows how long each component took and why it rendered. The <Profiler> component gives the same timings in code (onRender), e.g. for logging slow screens.

think.q: For 60 fps, how long can one interaction's work take on the main thread?
opts: About 16 ms per frame (less, since the browser needs time too)
why: Commits above that budget feel janky.

think.q: Why profile a production build (or profiling build) before drawing conclusions?
opts: Development mode adds checks and is much slower; numbers can mislead
why: Use react-dom/profiling for real numbers.

think.q: Which Core Web Vital measures how quickly the page responds to clicks and typing?
why: Slow React renders show up as poor INP.

think.q: The profiler shows React commits are fast, but typing still lags. Where next?
opts: The browser Performance panel: long tasks, layout, third-party scripts
why: Not every slowdown is a React render.

try.task: Write createRenderStats() returning { onRender, report() }: plug onRender into <Profiler onRender>; report() returns { [id]: { commits, mounts, totalMs, maxMs } } (round ms to 2 decimals).
try.hint: onRender(id, phase, actualDuration) → update an entry per id.

takeaway.key: Profile first (DevTools Profiler, production build), find slow commits and why they rendered, fix, re-measure.
